issues.legal_issue: The power to control exports includes the power to channel export trade through selected agencies or channels.
material_facts: The challenge concerned export controls imposed under an order made pursuant to legislation empowering the government to prohibit, restrict, or otherwise control exports.
The order permitted licensing authorities to channel exports through special or specialised agencies or channels.
issues.conclusion: The export-control legislation authorised canalisation, and the relevant provision of the order was within the delegated rule-making power.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947 conferred broad power to prohibit, restrict, or control exports. Control over export quantities may necessarily extend to persons participating in the trade, including their classification and the conditions on which they may export; canalisation is one method of exercising that control. The Court relied on Glass Chatons Importers and Users Association v. Union of India, which had upheld the constitutional validity of the canalisation provision.

predicates.export_control_case: The proceeding challenges a measure governing the export of goods.
predicates.government_controls_export_trade: The government regulates whether, how much, or through whom goods may be exported.
predicates.channeling_selects_export_participants: The measure directs exports through selected participants or channels, thereby excluding other participants.

issues.definition: When an export-control case concerns government regulation that channels exports through selected participants, the export-control power includes authority to use that method.

issues.legal_issue: Selecting a public trading agency as the principal export channel and excluding new entrants was not shown to be an unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on business in the circumstances of the export trade.
material_facts: The commodity had a very limited domestic market, and most production was intended for export.
The government sought to improve foreign-exchange earnings and maintain regular supplies of consistent quality to foreign buyers.
The government selected a public trading corporation as a principal export agency and granted it export quotas on an ad hoc basis.
Mine-owners without export performance during the specified earlier years were excluded from direct participation and had to sell to authorised exporters or the public corporation.
The appellant did not establish that the established exporters were improperly included or that the selected corporation was an unsuitable channel for the stated export objectives.
issues.conclusion: The selection of the public trading corporation and the resulting exclusion of new entrants were legally permissible in the circumstances; no legally enforceable right of the appellant was violated.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) guarantees the right to carry on business, subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public under the first part of Article 19(6). Canalisation necessarily excludes some groups, and a person does not establish an unlawful restriction merely by showing that they were excluded. The government may consider the nature of the commodity and trade, foreign-market requirements, continuity and quality of supply, and the suitability of selected agencies. The Court distinguished the State-trade provision in Article 19(6)(ii): the challenged arrangement was sustained as a reasonable restriction under the general part of Article 19(6), rather than as a statutory grant of a State monopoly.

rule.if: export_control_case and canalization_is_authorized and public_export_objectives_exist and selected_agency_is_suited_to_those_objectives and participant_classification_has_a_rational_basis

predicates.export_control_case: The proceeding challenges restrictions on participation in the export trade of a commodity.
predicates.canalization_is_authorized: The applicable export-control framework permits exports to be channelled through selected agencies or channels.
predicates.public_export_objectives_exist: The government is pursuing public objectives such as improving export earnings or ensuring regular supplies of suitable quality to foreign buyers.
predicates.selected_agency_is_suited_to_those_objec: The selected agency is considered likely to advance the stated objectives better than other available channels.
predicates.participant_classification_has_a_rationa: The groups permitted or excluded from export participation are distinguished on grounds relevant to the nature and circumstances of the trade.

issues.definition: When authorised canalisation serves public export objectives, the selected agency is suited to those objectives, and participant groups are rationally distinguished, excluding a group is a permissible reasonable restriction.

issues.legal_issue: An agency may qualify as a special agency for export canalisation because it is selected to advance the purpose of canalisation, even if it lacks prior specialised experience in that trade.
material_facts: The export-control order allowed canalisation through special or specialised agencies or channels.
The public trading corporation was selected to help maintain continuity of trade and secure exports in adequate quantities and of proper quality.
The corporation did not need to possess the same prior export experience as established private exporters to meet the meaning of a special agency.
issues.conclusion: The public trading corporation could be treated as a special agency or channel within the meaning of the order.
issues.legal_principle: The term “special” does not require an agency to have prior expertise in the particular export trade. In context, an agency is special when it is selected with regard to the purpose of canalisation and is more likely than other agencies to achieve that purpose, or to achieve it to a greater extent.

rule.if: export_control_case and order_allows_special_export_channels and agency_selected_for_channeling_purpose and agency_likely_to_advance_that_purpose

predicates.export_control_case: The proceeding concerns the legal meaning of a provision governing channels for exporting goods.
predicates.order_allows_special_export_channels: The governing measure permits exports to be channelled through agencies designated for a particular purpose.
predicates.agency_selected_for_channeling_purpose: The government selects an agency having regard to the objective for which exports are being channelled.
predicates.agency_likely_to_advance_that_purpose: The agency is considered more likely than other available agencies to achieve that objective or to achieve it to a greater extent.

issues.definition: An agency selected for a channeling purpose qualifies as a special channel when it is likely to advance that purpose, even without prior trade-specific expertise.

issues.legal_issue: A canalisation policy that leaves producers with no viable market, no assured purchaser, and no safeguards for fair allocation or prices may impose an unreasonable restriction on their business rights.
material_facts: The dissent considered a commodity for which there was practically no domestic market.
Producers excluded from direct exports depended on authorised exporters, and those exporters were not bound to purchase their output.
The authorised buyers could dictate terms, and the policy ultimately left the public trading corporation as the sole practical purchaser.
The policy did not provide definite rules guaranteeing producers a fair allocation, a reasonable price, or stable treatment.
issues.conclusion: In dissent, Justice Subba Rao considered the implementation of the policy an unreasonable restriction on the producers’ right to carry on business, although he agreed that the appeal should be dismissed because the requested licence period had expired.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 19(1)(g), a restriction on business must satisfy the general public-interest and reasonableness standard in Article 19(6). Article 19(6)(ii) does not itself authorise a monopoly by administrative action, although administrative interference may still be assessed under the general reasonableness standard. The dissent relied on Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P., [1955] 1 SCR 707, 727, in discussing the constitutional protection of business rights, and considered that a canalisation scheme should provide definite safeguards for fair allocation and prices.

rule.if: export_control_case and producer_has_no_viable_domestic_market and authorized_buyers_need_not_purchase_output and policy_creates_a_single_practical_buyer and fair_allocation_and_price_safeguards_are_absent

predicates.export_control_case: The proceeding challenges a policy restricting producers’ access to export markets.
predicates.producer_has_no_viable_domestic_market: The producers cannot realistically sell their output in a domestic market.
predicates.authorized_buyers_need_not_purchase_outp: The persons permitted to export are not required to buy the producers’ goods.
predicates.policy_creates_a_single_practical_buyer: The restrictions leave one buyer as the producers’ only practical outlet.
predicates.fair_allocation_and_price_safeguards_are: The policy provides no definite safeguards ensuring fair allocation, prices, or stable treatment for affected producers.

issues.definition: When producers lack a domestic market, the policy leaves them dependent on an unbound single practical buyer, and fair-treatment safeguards are absent, the policy is an unreasonable business restriction under the dissenting view.
